newsitem.title: INDIA: Rupee "overvalued" by 14 pct- India central banker.
newsitem.headline: Rupee "overvalued" by 14 pct- India central banker.

text.p: The Indian rupee is overvalued against major world currencies, as a result of heavy foreign capital inflows and despite persistent central bank intervention to brake the rise, a central bank official said on Friday.
Deputy Governor Y.V. Reddy of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said the rupee's strength could be one reason behind the country's flagging export growth.

"The overvaluation has got exacerbated with the sharp appreciation of the US dollar against the other major currencies -- the Deutsche mark and the yen," Reddy told a meeting of the Forex Association of India in Goa.

For most of 1996, Reddy said, the REER (Real Effective Exchange Rate) was stable, but last April, the trade-based REER (1985=100) rose to 65.41, about five percent over the August 1996 figure of 62.26, and ten percent over January 1996.
"Presently, compared to March 1993, the appreciation of the Indian rupee in real effective terms is around 14 percent," Reddy added.

Reddy said the Indian economy has certain favourable factors in terms of a moderate Current Account Deficit-GDP ratio, high foreign exchange reserves and a much lower ratio of short-term debt to reserves than that of many East Asian countries.
The rupee closed at 31.725/75 on Thursday. Markets were shut on Friday for the 50th anniversary of India's independence.
Dealers attending the meeting noted the central bank dollar buying only represented a rearguard action in order to keep the rupee below 35.70 against the U.S. currency.

"(The)35.70(level)is the benchmark. The RBI is going to continue this passive intervention (dollar buying) otherwise the rupee is probably going to grow stronger," Moses Harding, chief dealer at IndusInd Bank, a major player in India's currency market, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV) in an interview from Goa.
"There is no question of a depreciation of the rupee unless some active measures are taken to create demand for the foreign currencies here," Harding said.
Waves of foreign capital inflows have helped India's foreign exchange reserves rise to $29.8 billion as of August 1, equivalent to seven months of imports, Reddy said.
"This is equivalent to about 30 months of debt service payments, and nearly six months of payments for imports and debt service taken together," he added.

But currency dealers said the quality of the reserves is questionable, as fund managers controlling a lot of the capital inflows could easily sink the rupee and overwhelm any RBI support if they became disenchanted with India.
Early this week market regulator, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), said investments by FIIs had totalled $365.5 million in June, as compared to $198.4 million in May.
Cumulative net investment by registered FIIs in India totals $8.32 billion, it added.
In the meantime, the rupee remains a bastion of strength while South East Asian currencies crumble and south Asian neighbours pursue crawling devaluation strategies.
Reddy said India remained insulated from the woes afflicting the South East Asian economies.

"It is unlikely that any turmoil in South East Asian economies would have a direct impact upon the Indian rupee as India's trade with the five countries of the region (Thailand, Malaysia, the Philippines and Singapore) constituted only 7.8 percent in 1996/97," Reddy said.
Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) would soon be able to invest in Indian treasury notes as well as bonds, he added.

Global investment bank Merrill Lynch said in a recent report that Indian exports grew at only four percent in 1996/97 (April-March) against an 18 percent average growth rate for the previous three years.
